title: $0.0733, 10 minutes, Chinese model: You don't need Astra, you need rules
author: Massive-Guest-561
selftext:
I've been working on a small AI-based company I created last year, after graduating from University. 



Today I decided to start a side project to not get bored with pure python.



I was a bit scared because I'd never touched a video games engine, so I gave the agent the rules of my company repo and asked for something basic. It worked.



The rules are simple: short files in organized folders, headers in the files, tests thought for an AI agent, double check for the AI, well organized documentation, DDD and SOLID principles, etc.



I know this is so basic, but AI is just a machine reading your repo, outputs, logs and documentation and trying to do its best,



Hope it helps someone. I'll keep working on this.



Pd: The engine is Godot and the model is MiniMax-M3 in thinking mode. The agent is OpenCode

Pd2: I recognize Astra is powerful, but most of the time will be spent walking, not using a moon-rocket

  
I wrote you the skill I've used: [arodoo/basic-game-skill](https://github.com/arodoo/basic-game-skill)

comments.author: klas-klattermus
comments.body: It's my experience too. Most of the stuff I do doesn't need frontier models, it needs a good specification. It's fast and smooth though so as long as the company pays for it I'll ask Astra to change the color of the button

comments.author: LoveOrder
comments.body: astra great for 3D modeling + coding, but a bit pricey for coding compared to the alternatives

replies.author: TonyDaDesigner
replies.body: I just had astra 3d model an indoor environment based off a real location from a few pictures and I'm literally blown away with the result both 1) being so good and 2) taking only a few minutes.    Three years ago I hired a few artists to model some complex objects for a project. Not only did their work cost thousand of dollars, it also took awhile. I honestly believe that the latest batch of models just put 90% of those guys out of work. I can't see any feasible reason why I'd ever need to hire one again.

comments.author: RepulsiveRaisin7
comments.body: Duh, that's some basic ass 2d game any modern model can produce. And your instructions are in line with "make no mistakes", which doesn't really work, training > instructions. 120 LOC max per file is also pretty silly from a engineering perspective.

comments.author: TonyDaDesigner
comments.body: i used minimax 2.5, 2.7 and m3 quite a bit for game design. Used to have a minimax code plan and used it a lot.  I found it nearly unusable compared to using codex/gpt.  Minimax was good for fixing bugs but for building something from scratch- absolutely horrendous. Minimax is killing it with video/audio gen but it's really gotta be one of the worst for game design by a BIG margin.  I had better results with Qwen 3.5 and 3.6 running locally too (Despite taking a lot longer).    I know that you don't "need" the best models but I'd def recommend you try some other models because I don't regret cancelling my minimax sub one bit.

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body:
The pushback here is right about half your rules and wrong about the other half, and the line between them is worth naming.

Short files, headers, organized folders are style requests. The model honors them while it has room to pay attention and quietly stops when context fills. Those really are close to "make no mistakes", and training does beat them.

The rules that hold are the ones the model cannot violate because something else refuses: a test that fails, a linter that errors, a schema that rejects the call. Those work with a cheap model precisely because the model is not being asked to remember them.

I ran into this hard on a different project, a text RPG where a model narrates. Every rule I wrote as prose in the system prompt got broken eventually, including the ones I had shouted in capitals. What fixed it was removing the model's ability to write the numbers at all: it gets tool calls into an engine, and the engine owns dice, hit points and grid positions. It cannot fudge a roll because it never touches one. After that a cheap model was enough, same finding as yours.

So the version of your claim I would defend: you do not need a better model, you need constraints that fail loudly. Folder conventions are not that. Your "tests written for an agent to run" point is, and I suspect it is doing most of the work in your result.
